caseStudies.title: Training Designer: a course authoring and player app that replaced a paid product
caseStudies.pitch: When the authoring tool licence came up for renewal, I built the replacement instead.
context: The training team was producing eLearning in a paid authoring product. The licence cost more than £3,000 a year, the output format locked us in, and we used a small subset of the features: a block-based lesson editor, quizzes, media, and an export that played in the LMS. Course demand was rising (around 50 courses since 2022), and so was the number of people who needed to author.
built: A Rise-style course authoring and player application: a block editor for text, media, callouts, steps and knowledge checks; a media manager; themes and covers; quiz settings; and export to standalone HTML and SCORM, so courses run in the LMS without the original tool. Courses save in a documented JSON format, which later let me generate complete draft courses from source manuals with an AI workflow.
how: Built in phases, with AI assistance, against a written spec and a template export that acts as ground truth for the file format. The build-versus-buy call came down to three questions: do we use less than a third of the paid features, is lock-in costing us anything, and can the team maintain a replacement? Three yeses meant build.
outcome: Replaced a paid product, saving more than £3,000 a year.
The open format enabled AI-drafted courses from manuals, cutting first drafts from days to under an hour.
More of the team can author, because the tool is ours.

caseStudies.title: Workforce skills matrix: from a spreadsheet to the system sales decisions run on
caseStudies.pitch: Three generations of the same idea, each built when the last one stopped scaling.
context: A global laboratory services business with 200+ engineers maintaining more than 25,000 pieces of equipment had no reliable way to answer who is competent on what, where the gaps are, and who is qualified to train or assess others. The information lived in managers' heads and in site-level spreadsheets that disagreed with each other.
built: Generation one: an Excel matrix fed by Forms, to prove the data was worth collecting. Generation two: a Power BI dashboard joining competency data to the equipment hierarchy across 25,000+ assets, so gaps showed by site, equipment class and engineer. Generation three: a purpose-built matrix application with self-assessment, manager validation and a competency scale tied to observational sign-off records.
how: Anchored everything to the equipment hierarchy rather than to course titles, so a competency means something specific and survives when courses change. Designed the competency scale with the trainers who would use it. Rolled out through site champions rather than from the centre. Kept each generation running until the next one was adopted.
outcome: Covers 200+ engineers; used for gap analysis, training planning and trainer selection.
Now informs sales decisions: the business can show a prospective client what capability it has near their site.
Observational checklists and sign-off records anchored to the same hierarchy give the matrix an audit trail.

caseStudies.title: Asset risk film and explorer: replacing a heavy dashboard with a 78-second answer
caseStudies.pitch: A risk register of a few thousand rows and a dashboard nobody could get a decision from, turned into a short film that ends in the answer.
context: The laboratory estate of an R&D sciences client had been risk-scored asset by asset on criticality, age, breakdowns and obsolescence. The output was a generic dashboard and a slide deck: heavy, arithmetic left to the reader, and silent on the questions the client actually had. What do we replace, when, what will it cost, and which cost centre pays?
built: One self-contained HTML file in two halves. A 78-second film in six scenes walks from the whole estate to the handful of High-risk assets to a phased replacement budget. Under it, an explorer: the estate, each cost centre with a plain-English headline and a copy-for-email summary, and a filterable replacement list with CSV export. Behind both, a Python build recomputes every score, applies tier and budget rules from one documented config block the client can challenge, and fails loudly if anything does not reconcile.
how: Started from the questions a budget holder asks, not from the data. Built reconciliation in: estate totals against cost-centre sums against asset rows, and film against explorer, with an error on any mismatch. Found and explained a discrepancy between the earlier deck and the workbook rather than hiding it.
outcome: A few thousand assets across about a dozen cost centres reduced to three numbers and a phased budget.
Every figure traceable to its field and aggregation.
One file, no server, with deep links to any scene, cost centre or filtered list.

caseStudies.title: Training Store: find the course by the instrument in front of you
caseStudies.pitch: Several hundred courses in the LMS and no way to search them by equipment. One file joined the LMS, the skills matrix and the asset table so an engineer can type a model number and see what training exists.
context: A global laboratory services academy had several hundred courses, curricula, tests and observation checklists in its LMS. The LMS search only knew titles, so an engineer in front of an unfamiliar instrument could not ask the one question that mattered: is there training for this? Managers could not see what existed either, and requests arrived as unstructured email.
built: A single self-contained HTML course finder on the intranet. It joins three sources: the LMS catalogue export, the skills-matrix mapping of courses to equipment, and the asset classification table, which adds thousands of model and series synonyms. Type a model number and the courses for its equipment type come back. Users filter, switch between Training and Validation, and export a selection as CSV.
how: The first Training Store was a Power App built in 2022: it proved people wanted one place to find training, but it only searched titles and lived inside the tenant. The rebuild started with the data. A Python script reads the three exports, resolves duplicates, nests courses under curricula and emits one JSON. A React app renders it as one static file, so IT has nothing to host.
outcome: Several hundred catalogue cards, most mapped to equipment.
Two dozen equipment classes and thousands of model synonyms searchable, so a model number finds its training.
Launched in August 2026 for a 500-plus-person business, replacing the Power App; rollout across the business is still under way.

caseStudies.title: A procedure library run like a codebase, with an operating pack for the AI that drafts in it
caseStudies.pitch: Markdown masters, a build, a checker, a register that is the only source of truth, and a read-first pack so every AI session works to the same rules.
context: A global laboratory services business was rebuilding its procedure framework: five document types across eight workstreams, drafted by several people with AI assistance and reviewed by a panel. Documents edited by many hands drift in format and acquire client names and invented steps, and nobody could say what an AI session had been told before it wrote.
built: A documentation-as-code library. Each document has a markdown master, built to Word and PDF. A checker runs the mechanical half of the reviewer checklist: structure, numbering, roles, banned words, client names and open VERIFY markers. A sync tool rebuilds the markdown from a reviewer's Word edits and shows the diff. A register records every document and generates the index. An AI context pack: reading order, writing rules, allowed roles, a glossary and six reusable prompts.
how: Made the register the definition of existence: a document not in it does not exist. Made invention a build failure, not a request: where a source does not support a statement, the writer marks it VERIFY with who holds the answer, and the checker flags any marker without a register row. Kept humans on dispositions, sign-off and issue, and automated everything mechanical.
outcome: 82 documents in the register and growing quickly, across eight workstreams; one command builds, checks, registers and indexes.
Every AI session starts from the same ten-minute pack; the checker, not the model, holds the standard.
About 2,300 lines of Python and six prompts that other people run without me.
